title: The elephant, again
hook: each hand knows only a part of the elephant (Masnavi 3)
tomorrow: why would a chickpea try to jump out of the pot?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shepherd's clumsy prayer and a prophet told he was sent to unite, not to cut off. He looks at the heart. Today, a room full of people who can't agree.
screen: `HE LOOKS AT THE HEART.` → `A ROOM THAT CAN'T AGREE.`

segments.voice: Two screenshots of the same argument, cropped differently, posted by two people who are each completely sure. You met the elephant in Rumi's Masnavi early on this path: people touch it in the dark, and each describes a different animal. Read it again and there's an odd detail. In Rumi's telling, nobody is blind. The people can see perfectly well. The house is just dark. Why would Rumi set it up that way? Why do people with working eyes all disagree?
screen: `TWO CROPS OF ONE ARGUMENT.` → `NOBODY IN THE ROOM IS BLIND.` → `SO WHY DO THEY DISAGREE?`

segments.voice: Here's the story in brief. An elephant is kept in a dark house, and people who've never seen one go in to find out what it is. The hand on the trunk says: a water pipe. The hand on the ear: a fan. On the leg: a pillar. On the back: a throne. Rumi didn't invent it. In the Udana, a Buddhist text, a version has men blind from birth. Rumi changes one thing, and it solves the puzzle. If the people were blind, the fix would be new eyes, which nobody can hand out. Since they can see, the problem isn't them. It's the light. Then comes his line: if each of them had held a candle, the difference would have gone out of their words. Not one candle for the loudest person. A candle in each hand. Rumi's readers hear the candle as the light of an inner sight, a light from God that sees the whole. But the shape of the puzzle works on an ordinary Tuesday too. When two people who can both see are arguing about the same thing, the first question isn't who's blind. It's how dark the room is, and what would bring more light: a question, a second source, the other person's full story. Each hand is on something real. Bring a candle.
screen: `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `RUMI'S PEOPLE CAN SEE.` · `THE PROBLEM IS THE LIGHT.` · `A CANDLE IN EACH HAND.` · then, large: `BRING A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: Choose one person whose view on something you only half know. Send them one open question about it, a real one, not a trap, and decide now that you'll read the whole answer before you reply. Then set the phone face down and sit, letting your own argument rest.
screen: `ONE OPEN QUESTION.` · `READ THE WHOLE ANSWER FIRST.`

segments.voice: The elephant: Rumi's story of sighted people touching an elephant in a dark house, and the candle that would end their quarrel.
Before the next argument: bring a candle, one for each hand in the room. Rumi's fifth story, three to go.

howItsDone: Sufi teachers use the elephant in the dark house to teach humility about one's own grasp of the truth and the need for inner light; other versions of the story are told outside Islam too.

fork.reveal: both can see; the room is dark. more light, not a louder hand, is what Rumi asks for.

original.note: Persian and Arabic: candle; the light Rumi puts in each hand in the dark house.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone's opinion is equally right.
what it means: each hand touches something real, but only light shows the whole; bring a candle rather than a louder hand.
what a scholar hears: Rumi sets the story among sighted people in a dark house; the Udana's telling has men blind from birth, so in Rumi the fix is light, not eyes.
guess: more light, so each part is seen in the whole
a louder voice that settles the argument
a vote that picks the most popular view
